entries.title: Red Death
entries.content:
In the green rooms of the Abandonarium

                       –– Lucie Brock-Broido

Red liquid

Pumped through the arm

Is it poison or is it blood

The red bell head

Cauldron of mourning

The jet of poetry, candied by time

Two gleaming red glass hearts

Beating in the sun

I touch them

Smell the pinked hyacinth

The very nature of things

The goddamn essence of things

Red Hell, Rosa Rubea

Burgundy awakening

The sparkling red elixir I drink

My mind suddenly flooding

With love and anger

The great illusions of our age

Don’t hold back

There is a spirit to things

Lioness, flamed in red

A witchcraft hung

Channeled

By confusion

Red blessings

Reddening kisses

My ode to beginning

What would you say, if you could

You stand in my living room

Still sleeping

Come back to me, Sister

Come back, Mother

Come back, I said, sadly

The airplane

The baby

Very small

And waving

entries.title: What to Read to Wake Up Your Brain
entries.summary: These books can ease readers into a season of work and hard thinking.
entries.content:
These books can ease readers into a season of work and hard thinking.

Summer is the ideal season for fun, frothy reads. On languorous weekends or hard-earned vacations, many people skew their literary diet toward lighter fare—fast-paced thrillers, steamy rom-coms—rather than, say, an in-depth history or an experimental novel.

But fall is fast approaching. For some, that means a return to school; for many others, it represents the end of the most leisurely time of the year. Whether or not you’re heading back to the classroom, you may soon be tasked with, or else seek out, a more vigorous reading regimen; generally, the autumn months tend to require more from our brain. But it’s useful, as Labor Day approaches, to have an on-ramp—a way of easing into that more intense intellectual mode.

These six books can help reacquaint the fall reader with the pleasures and demands of paying serious attention. Although none of them is especially strenuous—most are either brisk, bite-size, or divided into digestible parts—they are undeniably stimulating. Each will give your mind a much-needed burst of energy.

The Age of Innocence, by Edith Wharton

I came late to Wharton’s 1920 novel about a high-society love triangle in Gilded Age New York City—in fact, I read it only two months ago. I had gotten into my head that the writing would be too ornate for my liking, the settings and dialogue too stuffy. But classics tend to be classics for a reason, and The Age of Innocence snapped me out of my heat-induced inertia. Wharton’s witty, sophisticated sentences require and then amply reward sustained attention. Narrating the follies and frivolities of the city’s elite, she’s sarcastic and allusive, winking even as she dazzles with dialogue that verges on poetry. (The novelist Roxana Robinson once compared Wharton’s diction to a “sword wrapped in satin.”) Yet the universality of the novel makes it a perfect gateway for reengaging with foundational literature: Its core subjects are the timeless tensions between desire and obligation, and between self and society, expressed through a smoldering romance between forbidden lovers.

Any Person Is the Only Self, by Elisa Gabbert

One of the best entry points to rigorous reading is our own curiosity. Genuine interest is powerful; it can help readers move through the most daunting chapters or grasp even the most complicated ideas. As both a reader and a writer, Gabbert has always been guided by the compass of her inquisitiveness, perhaps never more so than in her wide-ranging third essay collection. The author’s sense of wonder stimulates the reader’s, and her primary subject—literature—may lead one to more invigorating reading. She is as erudite as she is earnest, and as she ponders Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein and Marcel Proust’s Swann’s Way, or the lives and work of Sylvia Plath and Rainier Maria Rilke, her passion becomes contagious. As she suggests in an essay about her classic-literature book club, it’s always worth finding time to have your own “intimate experience” with famous novels. Following the winding pathways of Gabbert’s mind might well show you to your next great read.

Enough Is Enuf, by Gabe Henry

Few books have made me laugh harder or more frequently than Henry’s exploration of the English language’s nonsensical writing system—one in which the spelling of words tells us precious little about how they’re pronounced—and the centuries of failed attempts to fix it. Enough Is Enuf chronicles some of the staunchest advocates of “simplified spelling” systems (including Teddy Roosevelt, Mark Twain, and the dictionary maker Noah Webster), each of whom attempted to streamline the haphazard rules of written English—a uniquely weird amalgamation of other, older languages. Henry’s book sits at the nexus of linguistics and history—two subjects that can be daunting, in many cases making for dry reading—but it is brisk and entertaining, full of archival images, clarifying examples, and hilarious anecdotes. By its end, you’ll likely feel grateful for the miracle that is your own literacy and eager to read more about quirky characters, both human and lexicographic.

Suppose a Sentence, by Brian Dillon

Each of the 27 short essays in this collection is inspired by a single sentence that captured Dillon’s imagination. For more than a quarter century, the critic has kept dozens of notebooks in which he copies down striking phrases he’s stumbled across. They vary widely in length, register, and complexity: the cascading clauses of Roland Barthes, a nine-word short-story opener by Susan Sontag, the prince of Denmark’s dying “O, o, o, o” in Hamlet. Each essay is a perfect introduction to its source material, providing both a hook (the sentence) and a primer (Dillon’s reflections) to an eclectic set of authors (who also include Gertrude Stein, James Baldwin, and Hilary Mantel). Dillon’s notebook exercise, I might add, could be just the thing to re-attune one’s brain to the wonders of the written word.

Practice, by Rosalind Brown

Brown’s trim novel takes place over a single day in the life of Annabel, an Oxford undergrad who’s trying to write an essay about Shakespeare’s sonnets. The paper’s due tomorrow, and it’s not going well: She’s constantly interrupted by roving, unruly thoughts and a very demanding body (she’s hungry, now she’s horny, and now she’s gotta pee). She’d planned to stick to a rigid routine—a 6 a.m. wake-up, a distraction-free morning of work, a break to walk through campus—but is consistently derailed. (Who among us?) Flashes of insight come, but nothing sticks; the poems will not yield to her. As the deadline approaches, we get an intimate glimpse of a mind both at work and at war. Watching Annabel try to push her intellect past new limits may compel a reader to do the same—or perhaps just to read the novel with the same close attention she pays the sonnets. As for whether she finishes her essay on time, I’ll disclose no spoilers here.

Guilty Pleasures, by Arielle Zibrak

The smutty hockey romance Heated Rivalry is passionately beloved, yet many of its fans admit to being embarrassed by their obsession with the TV series and novels that inspired it. (Ardent and committed lovers of other things—such as, say, hockey teams—tend not to feel the same way.) But Zibrak, an English professor at the University of Wyoming, insists that no novel, film, or show is more shameful, or less worth consuming, than any other is—and that even art dismissed as lowbrow has “much to tell us about ourselves and the world.” In this short, snappy tract, she confidently surveys the landscape of “guilty pleasures”—usually those written by, about, or for women—and unearths newfound complexity. She manages to cover the obscure 1850 best seller The Wide, Wide World as well as Judy Blume’s Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret, along with critical essays from thinkers such as Hilton Als and Saidiya Hartman; each volume mentioned is worth tracking down. So are other volumes in the series this belongs to, NYU Press’s Avidly Reads.

​When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

entries.title: A Society of Cheats
entries.summary: Students’ use of AI is teaching them to cut corners, disdain rules, and believe that integrity is for suckers and wimps.
entries.content:
Students’ use of AI is teaching them to cut corners, disdain rules, and believe that integrity is for suckers and wimps.

Recently, I have taken to telling friends that whenever I’m on campus, I feel like I’m trapped in the middle of a crime spree. I’m not talking about an epidemic of overdue library books or out-of-control parties. I’m talking about AI and the ways in which students are constantly using it to cheat on any work that is assigned to them.

For those of us in higher ed—and I’ve taught at universities for more than 20 years—such widespread cheating is a baffling predicament. Universities are medieval creations. They are encrusted with eccentric customs, antique bureaucracies, and hierarchical privileges; any significant change typically comes about at a glacial pace. Not too long ago, I was still filling out grades in triplicate. I can liken the arrival of AI only to what it might have been like had a tribe of Neanderthals discovered a flying saucer hovering just outside their cave. To say that we were unprepared doesn’t begin to describe the experience.

By now, there have been many articles about how undergraduates’ promiscuous use of AI will affect their intellectual development, but I’m far more interested in its moral consequences. This is partly because I’m pretty confident about the former—I’ve told graduate students who actually learned how to write papers in college that I anticipate a generation of incompetents roughly a decade behind them—but also because I teach classes in leadership and business ethics, and I’m aghast at so many young people seemingly habituating themselves to cheating as a way of life.

Many students would no doubt object to this claim, but plainly that’s what they’re doing, cheating their way through their education. Every paper they don’t write, every problem set they don’t prepare, every serious reading they summarize into a memo—all of these are exercises in cutting corners, in getting by, and, at graduation time, in gaining a degree they didn’t earn.

That word is key: earn. To say that someone “earned” something is to apply a moral distinction to what one acquires. Not only can we get things we didn’t earn, but we can also obtain things we don’t deserve. The first is the good fortune of the trust-fund kid, the second the province of a thief.

Students are spending a lot of time learning to be thieves nowadays, and once they receive their dubious diplomas, they will enter the “real world” with all the qualities of a criminal syndicate: a knack for cutting corners, a disdain for community rules, and an assumption that a spirit of integrity, and the sacrifices it assumes, is the reserve of suckers and wimps. We will be a society of cheats.

I began to notice the change in the winter of 2023, when some of the writing assignments for my classes at Harvard and the University of Chicago took on qualities I had never seen before: squeaky-clean grammar, a superabundance of bullet points, and fairly robotic reiteration of facts rather than the pleasing lurch of original thinking.

This is the horrid house style of AI-generated papers; initially, it was not only the clumsiness of these papers that made them easy to dismiss but also the fact that the students submitting them were outliers. No longer. A spring survey by The Harvard Crimson found that one-third of the graduating class admitted to “using AI for an assignment against instructor permission,” which is a fairly sanitized way of saying “using AI to cheat.”

That survey was of students who’d entered college in the fall of 2022, before the mass adoption of AI tools. When it comes to students who are just arriving on campus this semester, I keep thinking about a colleague who teaches freshman composition at the University of Chicago. In the spring, he told me that, across all of the sections he had led over the past year, he believed that only three of his students submitted assignments written without the help of AI. Three students. In a class whose explicit aim is to teach writing.

At least part of the reason for this pervasive use of AI appears to be well-founded confidence that cheaters will not get caught, and that if they do, the consequences will be minimal. Take, again, the Harvard survey I mentioned. Among those 2026 graduates who admitted to “using AI for an assignment against instructor permission,” 93 percent of them said their cheating went undiscovered. Of the remaining students, more than half of them said they faced no disciplinary consequences even after they were caught. Just 2.6 percent of these students who used AI “against instructor permission” said they paid any price for their offenses—which, on the whole, is pretty good odds for anyone who is tempted to cheat.

For those inclined to break the rules, “playing the odds” is hardly an unusual strategy. It’s the corrupt cost-benefit analysis of fare evaders, speeding drivers, and tax cheats. It treats community rules not as common obligations but as opportunities for risk assessment. In the face of some illicit benefit, the question is not one of right and wrong, but of the likelihood of punishment.

Such thinking is especially seductive when it comes to “victimless crimes.” We often use that term, a hazardous oxymoron, to describe activities in which any benefits to the offender seem to outweigh any potential injury to others. To would-be offenders, the moral appeal of carrying out such crimes can be quite powerful, especially when the harm in question is remote or uncertain. They know the good they would enjoy, so it seems unjust and even gratuitous that they should deny themselves the reward when no serious harm would come to others.

My hunch is that this is how a lot of students see the unsanctioned use of AI. No real damage comes to any other person when they use these tools to write a paper or complete a problem set. At the same time, especially in a world where everyone is doing it—even some of their professors—why should they put themselves at a disadvantage of time, trouble, and professional advancement?

Of course, such logic already accepts one kind of harm: a debasement of the academic experience. A recent case out of Brown University provides a bleak illustration. In the spring, Roberto Serrano, an economics professor, decided to change the exam format for one of his classes from in-person to take-home. This was a generous concession on Serrano’s part to the anxiety that many of his students felt about being back in the classroom after the mass shooting on campus in December. How did students respond? Once they heard about the change, enrollment soared. Nearly 90 students signed up for a class that had never had more than 30 before, and the average score on the midterm was 96, with 40 students “achieving” a perfect score.

One doesn’t need the training of a tenured economist to know that this result is improbable. As Serrano told Insider Higher Ed, he ran his exam through ChatGPT and got answers similar to those of his unusually impeccable pupils—“kind of correct,” he said, but “with a very convoluted style.” And so, for the final exam, he switched back to an in-person format. Eighteen students immediately dropped the class. Nine students who remained did not take the exam at all. And among those who did, the average score was 48.6, the lowest average for a final exam in the history of his class by nearly 20 points.

Serrano was understandably sore. “We cannot afford to have a society in which a significant fraction of our best young minds think that cheating is OK,” he told Inside Higher Ed. “That leads to a declining society, to a failed society.” The specific failure he had in mind is intellectual—“We cannot choose to become idiots”—but the episode encapsulates the kind of moral rot that sets in whenever members of a community stop regarding rules as obligatory.

Set aside the offenders. For students in class who actually care about a subject, they know that they are surrounded by peers who are constantly cheating on their coursework. For professors who are excited to communicate new ways of thinking, they have to face a wall of young people who won’t make even the barest effort to understand the subject matter. And for graduate students who are working as teaching assistants, they have to spend hours each semester grading bogus assignments, at the end of which they face the prospect of having to give out a passel of underserved A’s.

This is the upshot of the crime spree under way at campuses across the country and around the world. It doesn’t involve the same type of harm as spiking the water supply or setting a building on fire—harm that is immediate, overwhelming, and undeniable—but, in the long term, it’s no less destructive. It entirely corrupts the integrity of an academic community, because learning in a classroom is impossible when everyone knows that the proceedings are ridiculous.

Glacial though they may be, universities are starting to respond. As The Atlantic’s Rose Horowitch reported in the spring, Princeton’s faculty voted to mandate proctors for all in-person examinations. The decision is the most significant change to the university’s famed Honor Code since it was first introduced in 1893, when the young men of Princeton successfully contended that their word alone should be enough to satisfy any concerns about cheating. For more than 130 years, students have had to attest: “I pledge my honor that I have not violated the Honor Code during this examination.” Henceforward, they will still be asked to do so, but it will be merely a formality. The faculty has decided that students simply cannot be trusted.

This is how communities tend to respond to crime waves: They beef up law enforcement. Surveillance widens, punishments stiffen, and legal codes expand to police behavior that was formerly restrained by customary norms of honor, decorum, and mutual reciprocity. As the superintendents of their academic communities, faculty find themselves having to prioritize the disciplinary elements of their job. They will spend more time serving as judge, jury, and executioner, even when what they really want to do is what they do best: research and teach.

A suboptimal allocation of academic resources may be the least we have to fear from this crisis in higher ed. Even if faculty can curb this wave of cheating—and count me doubtful—it is the result of an unprecedented number of students deciding that they don’t need to follow rules that disadvantage their own success and advancement, regardless of the implications for their peers and the corrosive effects on their community.

This is the mindset that young people across the country are graduating with, one less of strident careerism than of soft criminality. Relative to those who came before them, they will know very little, but they will be convinced of the wrong things, that the world will get along just fine without integrity in one’s work, trust in one’s peers, and pride in one’s community. These are all achievements, things you earn individually and together. You cannot steal them, but they can be taken from you—and they are being taken from all of us, faster than we know.

entries.title: Why Are So Many People Listening to a Podcast About Living in a Convent?
entries.summary: Dominican Sisters Open Mic has gone viral, in part because of its hosts’ unabashed joy.
entries.content:
Dominican Sisters Open Mic has gone viral, in part because of its hosts’ unabashed joy.

At a convent in Ann Arbor, Michigan, the bell chimes every day at 5 a.m. Then the 40 or so women who live there year-round—Dominican Sisters of Mary, Mother of the Eucharist—head to the chapel.

Their day begins with an hour of prayer, followed by Mass. At 7 a.m., they have breakfast together, in complete silence. Many of them head off afterward to teach at nearby Catholic schools—sisters, unlike nuns, are not cloistered—while the novitiates stay behind to study at “the motherhouse,” as they call the convent. On some days, one of the women—Sister Miriam Holzman, who started living there 20 years ago—turns to a new item on her schedule: podcasting.

Back in February, Sister Miriam started hosting Dominican Sisters Open Mic, a weekly show in which she and her fellow sisters discuss topics such as scripture, the saints, and day-to-day convent life. Sister Miriam told me that when the podcast started, she hoped it would encourage listeners to “go deeper in their spiritual life, no matter what their background might be”—Catholic or not, religious or not.

The show seems to have resonated outside Catholic circles. Clips of the sisters playing the ukulele and describing an Ultimate Frisbee match have gone viral on TikTok. As of late August, their account on the platform has more than 275,000 followers and more than 8 million likes. The podcast has been featured in The New York Times and on the Today show. Listeners seem to be especially drawn to the sisters’ cheerfulness. They laugh frequently and have an easy way of interacting with one another. “Their laughter seems so stress free,” one commenter observed. Another said, “Sisters, I also want that regulated nervous system laugh.” In a post liked by more than 5,000 people, one listener asked, “Why does being a nun seems so fun even though I’m not religious?”

Sister Miriam said that the show’s popularity may be connected to the overall trend of people seeking wellness content online. “People are looking for balance, and so are we,” she told me. “We want wellness too.” Their fixed routine—prayer, study, work, fun—minimizes unnecessary distractions. But the sisters aren’t just offering wellness advice or preaching self-optimization. Their search for balance includes trying to become a particular kind of person in body and soul, and noticing traces of transcendence every day. In one podcast episode, Sister Miriam talked about how, when she struggles to focus or when obligations and to-do lists intrude on her mind, her consistent schedule reminds her that in that moment, she is precisely where God wants her to be. “Which is such a gift,” she said. “I don’t need to be planning the rest of my life.”

Resisting the pressure to multitask or worry about the future seems to help the sisters prioritize prayer, a pillar of their Dominican order. At midday, the sisters meditate on the essential Christian belief that the all-powerful God took on human form in the person of Jesus Christ. Later in the afternoon, they recite the Liturgy of the Hours, a set of reflections on the Psalms and Gospels. Many of the sisters have said that after years at the convent, these practices spill over into the rest of their life—when they pray for a passerby at the airport, perhaps, or let out a sudden “Come, Holy Spirit” or “Jesus, I trust in you” at difficult points of the day. Prayer, a sister concluded in one episode, “expands your vision of reality.” It has allowed her to notice “the dew on the grass, or the sunrise on the way to work.”

As evening approaches, the sisters return to the motherhouse. They pray the rosary and have dinner together as one of them reads aloud from a recent papal address or a biography of a saint. Then out come the Trivial Pursuit boxes and guitars, the bicycles and Frisbees. As with prayer, recreation time together is fixed in their schedule. It’s not optional. The sisters don’t watch TV during it, nor do they scroll on phones.

For all the joy that the sisters display on the podcast, they are also open about the sacrifices involved in convent life. They seldom see their families. Their daily lives downplay individuality: Their sleeping quarters, called “cells,” are designed to be interchangeable and are minimally arranged with a bed, a dresser, a table, an image of the Virgin Mary. Adjusting to the 5 a.m. wake-up call can take years. And like all of us, the sisters are prone to stress and worry.

The contentment that the sisters seem to have despite these challenges may be partly explained by the documented benefits of engaging in religious practices. Clay Routledge, a social psychologist who studies sources of meaning in people’s lives, told me that prayer’s “cognitive and motivational power” can make people more attentive. He added, “It focuses your attention on something; it takes you off of these other distractions and worries, and helps you pay attention to what you care about.” In a 2016 study, psychologists at Georgia State University found that prayer motivated very religious students to “invest a greater amount of mental energy in the performance of everyday tasks.” A study from 2012 found that praying for others made participants feel more satisfied about making sacrifices for others—about living, in other words, a less self-oriented life.

Starting at 8 p.m., after their evening prayer, the sisters spend the rest of their night in complete silence. Sister Miriam told me that during this time she likes to pray about both the difficulties of the day and the things she’s grateful for. Another sister said that she sometimes walks up a nearby hill, notices the twilight sky, and thinks of her Creator. Then she returns to the motherhouse, ready for the next morning’s bell to chime.

entries.title: Roy Cohn Did It First
entries.summary: The debasement of American politics didn’t start with Donald Trump.
entries.content:
The day after Donald Trump won the 2016 election, the conservative political operative Roger Stone was among the lucky few to get through to him on the telephone. The president-elect reminisced about the long-dead friend who had introduced him to Stone: “Wouldn’t Roy love to see this moment? Boy, do we miss him.”

“Roy” was Roy Cohn, who became notorious in the early 1950s as chief counsel to Senator Joseph McCarthy and then built a career as a lawyer and fixer for New York City’s rich and powerful. His roster of clients, many of whom doubled as his friends, included Cardinal Francis Spellman, George Steinbrenner, the media mogul Si Newhouse, and a host of famous mafiosi, including “Fat Tony” Salerno and John Gotti. Trump met Cohn in 1973, when the young developer sought advice about a federal lawsuit alleging racial discrimination by his family’s real-estate company. Cohn proposed countersuing the feds for defamation—even though the company had been marking the applications of prospective Black tenants with a large C, for “colored,” and then telling them no apartments were available. The countersuit, for $100 million, failed as a legal tactic—the company settled with the Justice Department, without admitting wrongdoing, after two years of litigation—but it made headlines, which was the real point. Trump and Cohn had the same attitude toward the law: It was not a system of rules, but a way of getting what you wanted.

For a generation of liberal Manhattanites, the mere mention of Cohn’s name produced a visceral loathing. They saw him as a self-serving and unprincipled social climber whose crusade against communism had ruined lives. In documentaries, profiles, and the play Angels in America, he has been portrayed as a villain in the vein of Shakespeare’s Richard III, whose monstrousness can be traced back to his own sense of social exclusion. When Cohn contracted AIDS, he kept his illness and his sexuality secret to the end. He died in 1986 insisting that he had liver cancer, even while enrolled in a clinical trial to receive AZT, an early AIDS medication.

In American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey From Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump, Kai Bird—writing with his wife, Susan Goldmark, whom he credits with contributing significant research—aims to bring Cohn into focus as a progenitor of Trump. Bird’s previous work as a biographer has focused on distinguished statesmen and scientists of the mid-20th century, most notably the left-leaning nuclear physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, whom he and Martin J. Sherwin wrote about in American Prometheus, the book adapted by Christopher Nolan for the movie Oppenheimer.

Cohn, like Trump, had nothing but contempt for the norms and ethos of that mid-century elite. But Bird argues that this hatred was driven less by a coherent politics than by “dishonesty, narcissism, careless cruelty, and vengefulness.” Both men were avatars of the glitzy New York of the ’70s and ’80s, sharing an obsession with sex, a love of celebrity, and a hatred for expertise. Bird quotes the New York Times reporter Sam Roberts on the lessons Trump learned from Cohn: “1. Never settle, never surrender. 2. Counterattack, counter-sue immediately. 3. No matter what happens, no matter how deeply into the muck you get, claim victory and never admit defeat.” (Bird also implies that Cohn may have had a crush on Trump, blond and blue-eyed men being his ideal type.)

In Bird’s telling, the parallels between Cohn and Trump begin with their childhoods. Both grew up in New York’s outer boroughs, in families that were prosperous but resentful of those in the real inner circle. Cohn, born in 1927, lived in the Bronx as a young boy, the only child of a loveless marriage. His maternal grandfather, a wealthy banker, founded the Bank of United States, whose clients were primarily Jewish immigrants. Cohn’s father, active in the Bronx Democratic machine, agreed to marry his mother in return for being made a judge, which her father could promise thanks to his political connections. But the family was plagued by a scandal: The bank collapsed in the early years of the Depression, and Cohn’s maternal uncle, who had taken over as its president, was convicted of fraud and sent to prison at Sing Sing.

Cohn grew up without many friends; one of his cousins said that he was the kind of kid who would have enjoyed keeping a snake as a pet and feeding it live mice. His social life didn’t improve when the family moved to the Upper East Side in 1935. Few Jews lived in the area then, but the collapse of real-estate prices in the Depression made it possible for the Cohns to get a place on Park Avenue. Cohn was educated at elite private institutions: the Ethical Culture School and then the more traditional and uptight Horace Mann School, followed by Columbia for college and law school.

Thanks to his father’s influence, Cohn quickly got a job in the U.S. Attorney’s Office. He was soon working on high-profile cases against alleged Communists, including the writer Dashiell Hammett and the State Department official Alger Hiss. In 1951, Cohn was a key member of the team that prosecuted Julius and Ethel Rosenberg for conspiring to pass atomic secrets to the U.S.S.R. He intimidated Ethel’s brother David Greenglass, who’d worked on the Manhattan Project, into testifying against her. After the Rosenbergs were convicted, Cohn helped press Judge Irving Kaufman to give both of them the death penalty, hoping that Ethel would feel forced to talk. She did not, and the Rosenbergs’ two children were orphaned.

Cohn’s ferocious investment in anti-communism, Bird argues, reflected the fears of New York’s “Park Avenue Jews,” who worried that Jewish Americans would be suspected of disloyalty because of Lower East Side radicals like the Rosenbergs. It also made him a natural choice when McCarthy, then at the height of his anti-communist campaign, needed a new chief counsel. Cohn was hired at age 25, beating out Robert F. Kennedy for the job. He advised McCarthy as the senator oversaw more than 110 closed-door hearings and subpoenaed hundreds of people, many of whom lost their job or faced public humiliation.

Cohn was especially nasty toward gay men. Hundreds of federal employees were fired not for being Communists but because they were suspected of being gay. Not that the two were entirely separate in his view; Cohn, like many others, believed that homosexuals were prime “prey” for spies. At the same time, he was the target of homophobic rumors himself, especially about his relationship with David Schine, a wealthy, Harvard-educated young man whom Cohn persuaded McCarthy to hire as an unpaid consultant. When Schine was drafted into the Army as the Korean War was ending, Cohn tried to get him excused from basic training. After these efforts were rebuffed, Cohn called the Army’s general counsel and threatened to “teach the Army what it means to go over my head.” A month later, Army representatives were called before McCarthy’s congressional committee for the first time, setting up a confrontation that would eventually lead to McCarthy’s downfall. Bird argues that Cohn’s willingness to say and do anything to get what he wanted—no matter who might suffer along the way—provided a model for Trump’s approach to political life.

Cohn may have entered American political history because of his role in the Red Scare, but American Scoundrel emphasizes the career he went on to build in New York, where he showed an amazing capacity to escape legal repercussions for his misdeeds. Over the course of the 1960s, the liberal U.S. Attorney Robert Morgenthau unsuccessfully brought charges against Cohn for perjury, obstruction of justice, mail and wire fraud, conspiracy to bribe a city official, extortion, and blackmail. Cohn claimed that he was being targeted by Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, his old rival: “A few people are out to get me,” he declared. During Cohn’s second trial, his attorney suffered a heart attack. Instead of getting a new lawyer, Cohn gave the summation of the case on his own behalf, and when he was acquitted of all charges, he told the press: “Thank God we put juries between the type of tyranny that Morgenthau perpetrates on his enemies!”

Cohn could be charismatic. Ayn Rand fawned over him when they met at a party: “You’ve always fascinated me so much and I believe in so much of what you stand for.” Still, he comes off in this book as smarmy and unappealing, a cheat from start to finish. Bird gives us a litany of Cohn’s pettier sins. In the summer of 1968, he invited Cardinal Spellman and the Democratic politician Carmine De Sapio onto his yacht (named Defiance) to discuss judicial nominations, then wrote it off as a business expense. He and Barbara Walters were good friends and he hinted to gossip columnists that they were romantically involved, using her to hide his sexuality. Cohn had a lifelong habit of eating off the plates of his dining companions without asking their permission. He regularly stiffed his creditors. When one hapless small-business man sent him a memo reminding him of a $10,000 debt, Cohn scrawled a characteristic response: “Dear Louie: Fuck you. Roy.”

For Cohn, being gay was a private matter—his business, nobody else’s. Drawing on an unpublished memoir by Cohn’s cousin, Bird details sex parties at Cohn’s townhouse on East 68th Street; apparently the house was also used as the set for a pornographic film (Cohn owned two X-rated-movie theaters in New Jersey). He went out regularly to gay establishments, and the gossip columnist Liz Smith wrote that he “owned a number of successful gay bars around Manhattan.”

But Cohn remained intensely homophobic in public, telling people that he believed “gays shouldn’t be schoolteachers.” He lobbied against gay-civil-rights legislation for New York City in the 1970s and early ’80s. In 1978, he told an interviewer that anyone “who knows the way my mind works or knows the way I function in active life, would have an awfully hard time reconciling that with any kind of homosexuality.” The playwright Tony Kushner drew on this idea for the famous monologue that his version of Cohn delivers in Angels in America: “Homosexuals are not men who sleep with other men. Homosexuals are men who in fifteen years of trying cannot get a pissant antidiscrimination bill through City Council. Homosexuals are men who know nobody and who nobody knows. Who have zero clout. Does that sound like me?” the Cohn character asks. “No. I have clout. A lot of it.”

American Scoundrel offers an effective portrait of Cohn’s role in New York society in an era when sleaze and respectability were not clearly delineated. There is a great deal of salacious gossip; readers will learn far more than they ever wanted to know about Cohn’s sexual habits. Yet despite the extent of Bird and Goldmark’s research, the portrayal of Cohn as an unbounded narcissist misses some of what his life might tell us about the right-wing politics of his era. Earlier accounts have been more sensitive to the irony that Cohn was undone by the same political forces he rode to prominence. The repression of the McCarthy era—the frenetic demands for loyalty, patriotism, normalcy—helped bolster the sexual secrecy and homophobia that compounded the devastation of AIDS in its early years, cloaking the disease in fear and shame.

What Bird does give us is a new way to think about Cohn, Trump, and the legacy of McCarthyism. Cohn always presented himself as an outsider facing down a hostile, arrogant establishment, a stance that Trump adopted as he moved into politics. But Cohn’s career depended on being an insider, connected to New York’s media empires, real-estate developers, politicians, law firms, and private schools. Looking at the long arc of Cohn’s career shows how much of McCarthyism was about ambition and careerism, rather than ideology. His friends and clients were obsequious to him because they thought he could get them things no one else could: money, divorce settlements, political influence.

Cohn’s commitment to his clients kept him in rarified company until the end. In March 1986, Trump threw a bash for Cohn at Mar-a-Lago, inviting guests such as Lee Iacocca of Chrysler and Manhattan Borough President Andrew Stein. Cohn attended, his skin blotchy with sarcoma; afterward, housekeeping staff was instructed to disinfect the silverware with bleach. In late June, a little more than a month before Cohn died, he was disbarred in New York State for offenses including perjury, misappropriation of funds, and coercing a mentally incapacitated client into signing a will that appointed Cohn executor. A blue-chip roster of Cohn’s friends testified in his defense, including William F. Buckley Jr., William Safire, Barbara Walters, and Trump.

Cohn insisted he didn’t care about being disbarred. Recalcitrant and self-righteous, he always claimed to disregard other people’s opinions of him. He would have responded the same way to the conclusion Bird reaches in American Scoundrel, that he was an “empty vessel” with “no coherent personal philosophy unless you count his shallow mirroring of Ayn Rand’s celebration of unadulterated selfishness.” But he would surely have been bothered by the epitaph that was included on the AIDS Memorial Quilt—especially the last word: ROY COHN. BULLY. COWARD. VICTIM.

*Lead-illustration sources: Bettmann / Getty; Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress; John P. Kelly / Getty; Fred W. McDarrah / The New York Historical / Getty; vasiliki / Getty

This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Roy Cohn Did It First.”

entries.title: A Peaceful Detective Mystery to Watch
entries.summary: Culture and entertainment recommendations including The Sheep Detectives, the Hold Steady, and more
entries.content:
Culture and entertainment recommendations including The Sheep Detectives, the Hold Steady, and more

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Lily Meyer, a staff writer who has published stories about the wisdom of Holden Caulfield, why making America’s houses bigger may have been a mistake, and the Seinfeld theory of fiction.

Lily recommends watching The Sheep Detectives for a heartwarming mystery, listening to any song by the Hold Steady, and reading Brother of the More Famous Jack, by Barbara Trapido, if you want a good cry and a laugh.

— Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor

A good recommendation I recently received: My friend Eliza Brooke—a freelance culture writer who often covers movies—told me to watch The Sheep Detectives, which I had assumed was for children, but I trust her. I was absolutely charmed by the film and, at the same time, quite moved by its exploration of how we think and talk about death. Also, it’s a whodunit, and I love whodunits. Hollywood, could we please have fewer sequels and prequels and remakes, and more peaceful detective stories?

The upcoming arts event I’m most looking forward to: I can’t wait to see the Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock show opening at the Met this October. I love abstract expressionism, and ever since I read Mary Gabriel’s Ninth Street Women—an exceptional group biography of five abstract expressionist painters, including Krasner—I’ve been fascinated by the arc of her career, which included creating government-sponsored public art during the Depression, making mosaics in the Long Island house she and Pollock shared during their marriage (meanwhile, he got an entire barn as a studio), and the flowering of her own painting practice after his death. Of course I’m excited to see the Pollock paintings at the Met too, but I’m most eager to see the Krasners.

An actor I would watch in anything: Greta Gerwig. I saw Frances Ha, the gorgeous, bittersweet ode to female friendship that she starred in and co-wrote, a few weeks after I graduated from college—that is, at a moment when I was heartbroken about no longer living with my closest female friends—and I imprinted on her like a baby duck.

The best work of nonfiction I’ve recently read: Vivian Gornick’s The Romance of American Communism. Gornick, a “red-diaper baby” raised in the working-class Jewish Bronx, set out to interview former Communist Party USA members and militants about what their political activity meant to them, years after the party had lost most of its following. The result is a surprisingly beautiful and often wrenching reflection on belief, belonging, self-delusion, and sacrifice.

An author I will read anything by: Too many to name, so instead, I’ll give you a translator. I try to read—and believe I have read—everything that Megan McDowell translates. Her taste is impeccable, her style is flawless, and she works with some of the greatest Latin American authors writing today: Mariana Enríquez, Samanta Schweblin, Alejandro Zambra, and many more.

A quiet song that I love, and a loud song that I love: “It’s Gonna Be Easy,” by the Texas outlaw-country singer Doug Sahm, is a soft, melodic lament for a relationship the singer wishes would be easier to forget. (A recommendation to go with it: Callie Collins’s novel Walk Softly on This Heart of Mine, whose protagonist is loosely inspired by Sahm. Like the song, the book is a gentle heartbreaker.)

A loud song is “Waiting Room,” by my D.C. hometown heroes Fugazi. My husband and I asked the DJ to play it at our wedding, and the resulting mini–mosh pit is one of my favorite memories of the night.

A musical artist who means a lot to me: The Hold Steady. I’ve been going to their shows since I was 14, and seeing them live is the closest I’ve ever come to a religious experience. Hold Steady fans are real diehards, and the band’s lead singer, Craig Finn, believes fervently that—as he shouts at every single show—“we are all the Hold Steady.” He’s right: We are.

Something I recently revisited: I’m revealing a lot about my high-school self here, but one of my absolute favorite novels as a teenager was Chang-rae Lee’s Aloft, whose hero, Jerry Battle, is a New Jersey dad hiding from his emotions about family and aging by flying private planes. I revisited it before reviewing Lee’s new novel, A Tender Age, and was relieved that I loved it even more than I did at 15.

A favorite story I’ve read in The Atlantic: I’m not sure if “favorite” is the right word here, but Spencer Kornhaber’s essay about the singer Lizzo and her downward mobility has been haunting me since I read it. Spencer, I want you to know that introducing me to the concept of the Khia Asylum was not nice!

Something delightful introduced to me by a kid in my life: My toddler recently became obsessed with the book Chirri & Chirra, written and illustrated by Kaya Doi and translated from Japanese by Yuki Kaneko. It is so delightful. Doi’s illustrations are lovely, and the heroines’ sweet little adventure through the forest is a dream day. At the end, Chirri and Chirra go to a forest concert, and my daughter loves to sing “La-la-la” along with me as I read—it’s the best.

The last thing that made me cry: Brother of the More Famous Jack, by Barbara Trapido. It’s a sharp, generous tale of yearning and innocence, and its descriptions are my favorite kind, economical and precise. Its plot twist made me cry, but so did the intensity and joy of its narrator’s longing.

The last thing that made me snort with laughter: Also Brother of the More Famous Jack. I’m telling you, you need to read this book.

Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic:

The Week Ahead

  • Mayday, an action comedy about an American pilot stranded in Cold War Russia who teams up with a former KGB agent (out Friday on Apple TV)
  • Season 2 of The Gentlemen, a crime-comedy series about an aristocrat and his partner expanding their criminal empire into Italy (streaming Thursday on Netflix)
  • The Disappearers, a novel by Marlon James about a group of gay men whose lives are transformed after a mob attack in 1988 Kingston (out Tuesday)

Essay

We’re Living in the World Dolly Parton Built

By Spencer Kornhaber

Dolly Parton’s death at age 80 comes at a time when her influence seems at its peak. Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences seem hungry for honest idiosyncracy—for figures who, like Dolly, transmit their inner truth to mass audiences in a voice that’s clear yet scraggly. But Parton’s greatest legacy is existential in nature. Piling on wigs and feathers, she showed that you can be yourself while playing a character.

More in Culture

Catch Up on The Atlantic

Photo Album

Explore some weird, wonderful photos from the 20th century compiled by Alan Taylor last year.

Rafaela Jinich contributed to this newsletter.
