entries.title: The Golden Girls, but in a Camp Cabin
entries.summary: My weekend at adult summer camp
entries.content:
At Camp Social, where grown women return to girlhood, friendship has no preamble. Within 15 minutes of meeting eight of the campers from Cabin 3, I learned this: In their 50s and 60s, they have no use for the menstrual discs in the camp swag bag; one of them found online dating so depressing after her divorce that she’s given up entirely; when they laugh, they pee a little; they feel like they’ve known one another for years, even though most of them met last night.

The campers signed up for this weekend-long adult summer camp for exactly this purpose—to make new friends. On August 21, more than 400 women, some as young as 21, some older than 80, arrived at what usually is a children’s sleepaway camp in the Poconos to spend the weekend bunking in twin beds in log cabins, climbing the ropes course, developing middle-school-level inside jokes, making friendship bracelets, and performing choreographed dances at the flagpole to Cher’s “Believe” and Shania Twain’s “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” Everyone at Camp Social, regardless of age, is referred to as a “girl.” The camp promises to re-create a childhood experience so that grown-ups can bond with one another as easily as they might have as kids. I signed myself up because I wanted to know what kinds of adults would go back to summer camp and how seriously they would take it.

The girls of Cabin 3 were all in. When they were younger, they told me, making friends did feel more straightforward. But then they got jobs that kept them late at the office, or their kids grew up, or they stopped drinking, and the friendships they’d made with other parents or neighbors faded. They began wondering: How do you meet new people? Where do you go? None of these women ever really thought they’d end up at an adult summer camp, but they saw ads for it and thought, Maybe I’ll give that a try.

Which is how they found themselves at breakfast in the mess hall, cross-talking at Gilmore Girls speed, comparing notes on their adult sons, laughing when one revealed her favorite prank—taking a picture of her cleavage on the disposable cameras passed out at weddings. Over the hollering, Jackie Prendergast, a retiree who smiles so wide she shows both rows of teeth, told me that Cabin 3 had decided that its mascot for the weekend would be the flamingo. When a flamingo loses essential nutrients, as it does when reproducing, the pigment begins to drain from its feathers. With time and nourishment, though, the pink returns. “We’ve lost our color, but we’re going to get it back,” Jackie said. Ten minutes later, we headed to archery.

The night before, Camp Social’s girls had gathered in the barn for a dance where a band (all male, all handsome) played Prince, Michael Jackson, and Bruno Mars covers. Liv Schreiber, the camp’s 29-year-old founder, took the stage in her Camp Social shirt. “Welcome to camp!” she shouted, then launched into an ecstatic speech about the weekend ahead.

If anyone’s job could be described as “friend maker,” it is Schreiber’s. She is the type of person who skips more than she walks, makes it a point to memorize campers’ names, and, as I witnessed when we met up in New York City before camp, can form a real connection with strangers in a coffee shop in 10 minutes flat. She was working in real estate when she launched a viral matchmaking Instagram account and a matchmaking-party business, which morphed into events for adults to meet new friends. She opened Camp Social in 2023 to relive her own sleepaway-camp experience and to give women a place to meet. The waitlist, she told me, now runs north of 60,000 people.

Adult summer camps have been cropping over the past couple of decades—one even dates back to the 1970s—but many of them are co-ed and have the feel of either Club Med in the woods or an all-out bacchanalia. Schreiber’s is one of the only all-female options with an explicit friend-making focus. Bubble letters on the camp bulletin board read You Haven’t Met All The People Who Are Going to Love You; the camp’s tagline promises that “99% of campers arrive solo and 100% leave as friends.” To get the crowd riled up at that opening camp dance, Schreiber asked, with genuine enthusiasm, “Who wants to meet a new friend?” Hundreds of hands went up.

That “99% arrive solo” isn’t technically true. Mother-daughter duos and friends arrive together, and returning campers offer wisdom such as: Get to the Soffe-shorts distribution early to get your size, do not miss the Saturday pool party, and be sure to lean back right before the water slide spits you out into the lake.

Even so, Schreiber has designed the camp for people to make new connections. Before arrival, campers received a guide titled “How to Camp Social,” which encouraged them to reconnect with their childhood self—the person “who made a friend at the playground in four minutes flat, who didn’t ask if she was too much or not enough.” The camp’s “10-Foot Rule” says that if you’re within 10 feet of another camper, you should smile and say hi. Bunks are grouped by age, but other than that, women are encouraged to make friends outside their generation. The counselors (all female) are trained to be welcoming, Schreiber said. They dance with campers at mealtimes, cheer when someone reaches (or tries to reach) the top of the rock wall, and shout out “Camp Social?!”—a cue for campers to circle their hips and respond with a Kool-Aid-Man-style “Ohhhhh yeaaaahhhh.”

Who needs this kind of help making friends as an adult? Before I arrived, I’d wondered how many socially anxious people I might meet. Maybe the shyer campers were making themselves scarce, like Cabin 3’s mysterious tenth bunkmate, who kept to herself, or the girl in my cabin who disappeared when we all got ready for Saturday night’s camp disco. But most of the women there seemed capable enough of making friends; they were just in a moment in their life when opportunities to find those relationships felt scarcer. Compared with men, whose friendship skills are more often lamented, women do typically have more friends and are less likely to be severely socially isolated. But having a lot of friends doesn’t necessarily mean that a person’s social needs are getting met, and overall, rates of loneliness between the genders are roughly the same. The women at Camp Social were new mothers, grandmothers, empty nesters, divorcées, widows, and retirees; pretty much everyone was going through some kind of potentially isolating life transition. The average camper that weekend was 39 years old, an age when many people are taking care of kids and aging parents, which doesn’t leave much time for friendship.

For some attendees, camp simply functioned as a three-day lake vacation they didn’t have to plan—where they could do yoga on a paddleboard, attend an outdoor screening of The Princess Diaries, and drink signature camp cocktails. Last year, Schreiber told me, one woman in her 80s did nothing but archery the entire weekend. But many of the women I met came in order to feel like girls again, maybe with the hope that that would make friendship feel as easy as it did when they were kids.

For Cabin 3, Camp Social seemed to work a spell of quick intimacy. Of the cabin’s 10 girls, eight of them moved as a pack. (The ninth had come with her daughters and was spending time with them; the tenth I could never track down.) On the way to archery—along the lake and past the cabins, the pickleball courts, the pool, and the ropes course—the girls speculated about how someone would even use those menstrual discs, and Sandi Sullivan, who works for a construction company in Chicago, considered transforming her camp-branded bandana into a halter top for the camp disco, like the one her mom made her in the ’70s. When the archery instructor approached the group, he asked Vicki Petroski, a recent retiree, if she’d be a five—as in the fifth person on the range. “No, I’m a 10,” she replied. The girls cackled. The instructor blushed, and they cackled even louder. (Unlike the counselors, the camp’s staff members—who run the archery range, lifeguard the pool, and referee the camp Olympics—all seemed to be handsome 20-something men with British, New Zealand, or Australian accents.)

“In my 20s and 30s, I never would have talked so openly with other women I’d just met,” Jackie told me. It helped that Cabin 3 had all reached the age where, as Linda Gryn, a business owner from Pennsylvania, said, “We no longer give a shit.” Some of the girls rarely speak about sex with their friends back home, but here, thanks to Vicki, whose daughter is a sex therapist, somehow every conversation seemed to come back to it.

The group was too busy for awkward pauses, anyway. The girls danced: Linda, who had been a majorette in high school and dated a football player, watched the dance instructor like a hawk during morning flagpole routines. They painted (okay, while drinking mimosas) at the paint-and-sip. Vicki went tubing for the first time in about 30 years. “Everything I did was 30 or 40 years ago,” she said. “When I turned 60, I said, Fuck it, I’m having fun again.”

But being 60 is not always as fun as being 10. At the afternoon pool party, as girls from Cabin 3 and I waved at Vicki, in line for the water slide, Christine—the most reserved in the group, a sensible lawyer with a sensible black bob—came over to me. (She is perhaps so sensible that she asked me not to use her last name.) Going to an adult summer camp at all, let alone by herself, was not usually her speed, she said, and she already has a close group of friends. But recently, the man she’d been with for 40 years “decided he didn’t want to be married to me anymore.” One night, he said “I love you” before bed as usual, and then the next day, he told her, “We’ve had a good run, but I’m ready for the next chapter of my life.” A good run? Christine remembered thinking. I thought that I was happily married. Her adult sons were trying to stay neutral; she was trying to be okay with that.

Just then, Vicki went down the slide. The red-and-yellow half tube shot her multiple feet in the air, and we cheered when she emerged from the lake, grinning. Her curls were matted; the purple face paint she put on for camp Olympics was running down her cheeks.

Somehow, as the evening set in, everyone still had the energy for karaoke and the disco. The girls in my own cabin, all in their 20s, were getting along well, but if Cabin 3 had reached the peak of camp friendship, my cabin was still in the “friendly roommates who ask about one another’s day” stage. As we got ready to go back out, one bunkmate did my makeup; another, who had been to Camp Social three times, told me the “vibes were off” at the pool party this year because it was overcast. At karaoke, while other bunks performed as a group, we bobbed our heads and drank our alcoholic “Bug Juice,” garnished with gummy worms. Meanwhile, Cabin 3 was on fire. Sandi, whose camp-branded bandana she wore tied up as a headband after all, raged to Smash Mouth’s “All Star.” At the disco, they danced in sequins and jumpsuits to the songs that had been on the charts when Linda was in high school.

Then it was Sunday morning and time to go back to real life.

Before the last morning flagpole, campers swapped Instagram handles and phone numbers. People seemed to have made friends, although a couple of younger girls I spoke with told me they definitely had not. They were ashamed that, even in an environment set up for friendship, they hadn’t connected with anybody. Those who had made friends wondered whether they would see them again soon or if they’d be only “camp friends.” When I asked my bunkmates whether they thought they’d stay in touch with anyone, one of them said rather ominously, “Only time will tell.”

But over breakfast, the girls of Cabin 3 helped one another download WhatsApp and started a group chat. Since then, they’ve been trading photos of the shirts they had tie-dyed and group pictures from the disco. One of the girls, Jacqui Moore, had painted a flamingo at the paint-and-sip, which has stuck as the group’s symbol. “Keep your pink coming!” Linda wrote in one message. Three girls who live close to one another in Pennsylvania are planning to get lunch. Others might join one bunkmate walking a marathon. (In accordance with their flamingo theme, they say their team name would be “The Flockstars.”)

They probably won’t come back to Camp Social, though: The camp served its purpose. Maybe these women will get together annually to share the secrets they can’t with the people they see everyday. Maybe they’ll have a ball at Jacqui’s 60th birthday party. Maybe, like their other friendships, these will fade too. For now, they’re planning a reunion for next year. Greece—or maybe Moab?—could be nice.

entries.title: Which Dan Sullivan Will These Dan Sullivans Vote For?
entries.summary: The Alaska Senate race has become complicated by two candidates with the same name.
entries.content:
The Alaska Senate race has become complicated by two candidates with the same name.

What in the Dan Sullivan is going on in Alaska? Senator Daniel S. Sullivan is running for reelection. Daniel J. Sullivan is one of his challengers. And former Anchorage Mayor Daniel A. Sullivan recently endorsed the senator, while also declaring himself “the OG Dan Sullivan.”

“It’s kind of hilarious,” Daniel K. Sullivan, a 33-year-old diesel mechanic and off-road fabricator from Wasilla, who is not running for Senate, told me.

“I got a chuckle out of it,” Daniel P. Sullivan, a longtime teacher from Nome, who is also not on the ballot, told me.

Control of the Senate could come down to a ranked-choice ballot that currently includes two Dan Sullivans (the Republican incumbent and the Republican challenger) and one Mary Peltola (a Democrat who was the state’s former at-large congresswoman). Republicans are worried that voters could be confused about which Dan Sullivan to select. Theories abound: Is this some sort of nefarious political plot by the Democrats? Or is it just that there are so many Dan Sullivans in the state that something like this was bound to happen?

To get at the question, I reached out to half a dozen Dan Sullivans who appear to live in Alaska.

I caught a second Daniel P. Sullivan, this one from Chugiak, while he was driving on a remote gravel road the other day. “The Dan Sullivan thing” has become a common topic of conversation, he told me, and his co-workers call him “the senator.” So many Dan Sullivans live in Alaska that his firearms purchases require a deeper background check. “So I don’t get mistaken for another Dan Sullivan,” he explained. (He said that he’s planning to move next summer so likely won’t vote for either of the Dan Sullivans: “Not really fair to vote when the outcome doesn’t affect me.”)

Daniel F. Sullivan, a registered nurse, called me back from Palmer. “I often joke that I’m the real Dan Sullivan, and those are all imposters,” he told me. He said he grew up in New York with another Dan Sullivan in his high school, who was a better student than he was: “My parents would sometimes get honor-roll letters in the mail. I always wondered if his parents got all the bad letters about skipping school.”

In Alaska, he found that his name had even greater benefits. A few years back, he had workers out to fix the electronic system in his hot tub, and the bill they promised to send never arrived. “I often wonder if the other Dan Sullivan got the bill,” he said. Whenever he’s part of a group going out to eat, the reservation is in his name in case it prompts VIP treatment. In this election, he said, he’ll probably vote but hasn’t settled on a candidate. “I won’t vote just because it’s a Dan Sullivan,” he said.

This is not the first time a ballot has featured multiple Dan Sullivans. In 2014, Dan S. Sullivan was running for Senate for the first time when Dan A. Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, was running for lieutenant governor (the Senate bid was successful; the lieutenant-governor one was not). Then, in 2016, the former mayor briefly ran for the state’s other Senate seat. Had he won, both of the state’s U.S. senators would have been named Dan Sullivan. Neither of those Dan Sullivans returned my messages.

The Dan Sullivan who has put the name into the news is Dan J. Sullivan, who lives in Petersburg, a small fishing village on an island where Sitka black-tailed deer outnumber the roughly 3,000 people. His father was named Dan Sullivan. So was his grandfather. At the moment, so is one of his sitting senators. Shortly before the June 1 deadline, he filed paperwork declaring his candidacy. “We need a Sullivan who stands up for Alaska,” his website says.

The only Dan Sullivans he personally knows, he told me in an email, are in his own family: three Dan Sullivans and four more Dans who are not Sullivans. “We all have nicknames,” he said. “Mine will never be divulged.” He says that his campaign strategy mostly consists of maintaining his website and posting on social media. “Maybe some travel, but I don’t have much money,” he told me. (He has $8,400 cash on hand in his campaign account. The other Dan Sullivan has nearly $7.3 million.)

His candidacy was immediately challenged by the National Republican Senatorial Committee, which referred to him as “Sham Candidate Sullivan,” and the Alaska Republican Party. Senator Dan Sullivan told reporters in Washington that it was “an insult” and that the challenger was “trying to trick my constituents to rig the election for Peltola.” “This is serious stuff,” he told CNN. “When people are going, Oh there’s two Dan Sullivans, isn’t that funny? No. It’s cheating.”

The senator and his allies pointed to similarities between the challenger’s logo and the senator’s: Both are navy and mustard-yellow and feature at least one gold star. They accused the other Dan Sullivan of being part of a partisan plot engineered by a Democratic consultant. The Sullivan facing those questions told me the consultant had helped set up his campaign site and provided “tips on communications and basic campaign functions,” but said “she is not currently working for me.” They questioned his party affiliation. (He was previously a member of the Alaska Independence Party, but when that disbanded late last year, he switched his affiliation to the Republican Party, which he said was in line with his conservative views.) The director of the Alaska Division of Elections, which is overseen by the state’s Republican lieutenant governor, determined in June that the newcomer’s declaration as a candidate was invalid because it had been “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.” The Sullivan in question appealed to the Alaska Superior Court.

“I am running because I am tired of sitting back and watching our current Senator routinely fail to represent the interests of ordinary Alaskans like me,” he wrote in his defense. “The fact that Senator Sullivan shares my first and last names adds insult to injury, motivating me to raise my hand as an alternative choice for Alaskans.”

Ultimately, the court determined that Dan Sullivan met all the requirements for making the ballot: It was his actual name; he did live in Alaska; he was over the age of 30. The whole experience, he told me, has been “daunting” because he feels unfairly singled out. “Typical of Sullivan to cry about it, make a nickname, and blame others,” he said, when asked about being called a “sham” candidate. Of the dozens of candidates running statewide in Alaska, he said, “only I have been accused of bad intentions (including one guy who is in jail). Seems unfair to me.”

Both Dan Sullivans were on the ballot in the nonpartisan primary earlier this month, after which the top four candidates advanced to the general election. Peltola, the Democratic candidate, got the most votes, leading the incumbent Sullivan by seven percentage points. Daniel J. Sullivan came in a distant third with 2.5 percent of the vote, qualifying him for the general election—and showing that he could be a spoiler in November.

His advancement angered Republicans, including the president. “The Crooked, Radical Left Dumocrats have put up another man named ‘Dan Sullivan,’ and they did this to take Votes away from our Great Senator of the same name,” Donald Trump wrote on social media. Senator Dan Sullivan’s early campaign ads have not mentioned the other Dan Sullivan, and when he talks in his speeches about an opponent, he references only Peltola.

But this is not the first time an election has featured similarly named candidates and accusations of political shenanigans. When John F. Kennedy ran for Congress in 1946 against a Boston city council member named Joe Russo, his allies helped recruit a janitor named Joe Russo to also run. In 2004, Representative José E. Serrano of New York was primaried by an unemployed former dockworker, Jose E. Serrano, who dropped out after being questioned about his legislative platform and not knowing what that was. In 2024, the governor’s race in Washington State featured Attorney General Bob Ferguson running against Robert Arthur Ferguson and Robert Benjamin Ferguson (the latter two Fergusons withdrew from the primary before ballots were printed).

The name Dan Sullivan is common enough. There was the offensive lineman for the Baltimore Colts in the 1960s. There was the race-car driver Danny Sullivan, who won the 1985 Indianapolis 500. There’s a theater and film director named Daniel J. Sullivan. Daniel was the ninth-most-common first name and Sullivan was the 107th-most-common last name in the United States in 2020, according to census records. There are nearly 5,300 Dan Sullivans in the country, according to the personal search aggregator Spokeo, and more than two dozen in Alaska.

In Anchorage, there’s the Sullivan Arena (named for the city’s longtime mayor, George M. Sullivan, the father of the Dan Sullivan who was the most recent mayor of Anchorage) and Sullivan’s Steakhouse (named after John Sullivan, a 19th-century boxer). “Sullivan just seems to be the big thing,” Dan Sullivan the Wasilla mechanic told me. “But I don’t know any benefits from it that I’m aware of. I don’t get any discount at the steakhouse or anything.”

The Dan Sullivan from Nome told me he would occasionally get random calls from people around the state confronting him about his campaign promises, especially when the Anchorage mayor and the U.S. senator were both Dan Sullivans. “I’d show my credit card, and they’d look at me and do a double take,” he said. “I got to meet all the Dan Sullivans. All the famous ones. I’m probably the least interesting out of all of them.” (He has since retired and has been traveling, and says he has not yet done his homework on which candidate he’ll support in the election).

For the Dan Sullivans, it can be a little disorienting when the political ads are blanketing the airwaves. “It’ll say, Dan Sullivan’s ruining the Alaska fisheries! Or Dan Sullivan voted to raise your health insurance! I’m like, No, I didn’t! It wasn’t me,” said Dan Sullivan the mechanic. “Or you’ll get an ad on the radio and it’s like, Dan Sullivan’s great for Alaska! Yeah, he is.” He’s not much into politics, so he says he’s unlikely to join the other Dan Sullivans in campaigning. He’s more conservative, so he plans to vote for the incumbent senator.

As if things couldn’t get more confusing, there’s also a Dan Sullivan who has run for Congress in Massachusetts. There are so many Dan Sullivans that, at times, my attempts to reach the ones in Alaska went awry. I messaged a Dan Sullivan I thought for sure was from Palmer, Alaska, but instead located one in Cleveland, Ohio. He politely responded that his origins are in Brooklyn and Massachusetts. “I am Daniel M. Sullivan. My dad was Daniel P. Sullivan,” he said. Although he won’t be voting in Alaska, the intrigue has caught his eye: “I have been following this story with interest.”

The Alaska race will be determined in November. At least in this election cycle, there’s room for only one Dan Sullivan in the Senate (and possibly none). But some other Dan Sullivans are getting ideas about future options.

“Maybe one of us needs to run for president,” Dan Sullivan the mechanic told me. Or perhaps two? “You can pick anybody you want. As long as it’s Dan Sullivan.”

entries.title: This El Niño Will Be Unlike Any in the Past Eight Decades
entries.summary: Die-offs and floods have started already, a prelude to supercharged storms and droughts.
entries.content:
Die-offs and floods have started already, a prelude to supercharged storms and droughts.

In the middle of the Pacific Ocean, along the equator, scientists have drawn a box. It’s a big box, two-thirds the size of China, yet hardly anyone lives inside it. This rectangular swath of open ocean is monitored by satellites and a network of moored buoys that measure minute changes in the temperature of the water, with an eye toward anomalies. Every few years or so, driven by changing winds and currents, the water temperature in this part of the ocean starts to rise; even a half degree Celsius above normal over months warrants a designation that an El Niño phase has begun. That’s enough warming to unleash floods and fires, drought and famine, around the world. The box is called Niño 3.4. Right now, it’s hot in the box.

“Like a baby pool,” Kristina Tietjen, who spent most of August scuba diving in the middle of this mass of abnormally warm water, told me. Tietjen has been coming to the world’s largest atoll, Kiritimati, for more than a decade to study its coral reefs. She usually dives in a medium-weight wetsuit; this trip, her team needed only rash guards. It is still early in this El Niño cycle—which is likely to be the strongest ever recorded—but the waters around Kiritimati have already been 3 to 4 degrees Celsius above normal.

Tietjen’s time on Kiritimati (pronounced like Christmas) has allowed her to watch, in brutal detail, what these repeated warm-water cycles, playing out in a steadily warming ocean, mean for the great tropical coral reefs here, which were once near pristine. During her first El Niño, in 2015–16, 90 percent of Kiritimati’s coral reef died. Years of slow, partial recovery followed. This month, Tietjen and her colleagues, part of the Canadian scientist Julia Baum’s lab at the University of Victoria, discovered that nearly half of the island’s remaining corals had already bleached—a prelude, if warming persists, to death. When Tietjen comes back, she may well be swimming over a graveyard.

Most of the world experiences El Niño’s ripple effects as the heat building up in the equatorial Pacific radiates into the atmosphere and around the globe. This means great gouts of rain in supercharged storms in some places; in other areas, crop-killing dry spells that can extend for months. Along the Pacific Coast of South America, torrential rains and landslides have forced the temporary closure of a main route to Machu Picchu, in Peru; deadly floods have swept through arid regions of northern Chile. Countries such as India and Ethiopia are enduring some of their driest summers on record. El Niños tend to mean more rainfall across the southern United States and drier stretches across a band in the North. Strong El Niños can mean record-breaking heat, and this one is shaping up to be unlike any catalogued in the past eight decades. A 2-degree-Celsius increase in the Niño 3.4 box typically earns the title of “Super El Niño”; we’re already past that threshold, and experts project that the warming could peak at roughly twice as high. “We are now pretty certain this will be an exceptional event,” Malte Stuecker, the director of the International Pacific Research Center at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told me.

Part of the reason Stuecker expects this warmth to keep building is that the buoys along the equator can detect water temperatures well below the surface. Down more than 100 meters, an enormous mass of warm water has built up and will rise to the surface in the months ahead. The amount of heat brewing in the ocean has produced one of those graphs in which the current year departs drastically from past trend lines, wriggling up erratically into unfamiliar territory.

Although scientists continue to debate the extent to which climate change makes El Niño cycles more frequent or intense, they agree that these cycles are occurring in an ocean that is warmer than it was. Last Saturday, the daily global average sea-surface temperature reached 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit), its highest level on record, according to Europe’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Even if El Niño cycles are not changing at all, as they spiral around that ascending baseline, the temperature peaks they hit keep getting higher, causing repeated blows to marine life and disrupting ecosystems in ways that may be irrevocable.

Carlos Zavalaga, the director of the seabird lab at the Universidad Cientifica del Sur, in Lima, began to comprehend the magnitude of this year’s warming in mid-June, when he visited Macabi and Guanape Norte, two islands off the northern coast of Peru. He’d been hearing from colleagues about dead birds washing up by the hundreds on the coasts of Peru and Ecuador. He’s seen the news stories about flocks of hungry Peruvian pelicans swarming the fish markets in port cities looking for food. On the two islands, which just last year were thronged with pelicans, Inca terns, and Humboldt penguins, Zavalaga found empty nests, some with eggs and starving chicks. “They were abandoned islands,” he told me.

These seabirds feed on schools of anchovies swept up in the Humboldt current, the cold, nutrient-rich upwelling waters that create bountiful fisheries off South America’s Pacific Coast. During El Niño years, that current gets displaced by warmer waters pushing east across the ocean, and these great schools of feeder fish can vanish from the coasts. The decline has been severe enough that Peru this month shut down an anchovy fishery that is a key economic engine for the country, with much of the year’s quota unfilled. Long before satellite monitoring, Peruvian fishermen noticed these cycles of warmer waters and dwindling fish stocks; they named the phenomenon, which peaked around Christmas, after the Christ child. References to El Niño in Peru’s scientific literature date back to the 19th century.

In his three decades studying seabirds, Zavalaga has witnessed die-offs before. But it is the rapid-fire nature of these blows and the severity of the disruptions that make him so concerned. Just three years ago—the same year avian flu killed more than 500,000 seabirds—another El Niño slammed into the coast of Peru. The birds that had made a tenuous recovery since then now face the prospect of another die-off. “It’s like a boxing match: You have a first knockout, you try to recover quickly, and then you have a second knockout,” he said. “I cannot imagine what will be the scenario by the end of this year.” He doubted that the birds could go extinct, but some species might move farther south in search of colder waters. The coastline in Peru and the culture that depends on the fish and the birds could be permanently altered.



When the warming started around Kiritimati, one of the few populated islands in the Niño 3.4 monitoring zone, Bill Newton, an island resident, was fascinated by how evident the changes were. He told me that the normally dry island turned sopping wet, and regular floods started washing out the roads. The wet brought swarms of mosquitoes (prior El Niños have led to outbreaks of dengue and chikungunya) but also clouds of dragonflies, which he hadn’t seen before. Higher-than-normal tides poured into seafront homes. Tuna, which can do well in warmer water, attracted dozens of fishing boats off the coast. Prevailing winds changed direction.

Corals have a particularly hard time when water warms; they can’t move elsewhere, and they are sensitive to heat stress. As little as four weeks in water just a degree warmer than normal can cause bleaching, the loss of the symbiont algae that supply corals’ food and brilliant colors, according to Baum, whose lab Tietjen works at. Baum, an ecologist, has studied Kiritimati’s reef since 2009. After the El Niño a decade ago killed off nearly the entire reef, Baum began to consider the possibility that she would witness the obliteration of an ecosystem in her lifetime. In a 2018 paper in Science, she projected that successive bleaching events could occur frequently enough that coral reefs, which take roughly 10 to 30 years to recover from mass mortality, would not have time to regrow. In the years since, she had been hopeful that nature could fight back as she watched surviving corals take up symbionts that were more heat resistant. This year’s warming and the pace of bleaching already under way have dispelled that hope.

What happens next is in some ways predictable. El Niño is not a haphazard force of destruction; it’s a warming phase in a specific area in the Pacific Ocean that scientists have determined shifts the probabilities for certain weather outcomes in various parts of the world. Those probabilities are reliable enough that, for example, the U.S. Navy already plans to send a hospital ship to the coast of Peru in February to be in position to help after expected floods. But as Baum and other scientists who study and love the delicate ecosystems in the equatorial Pacific are finding, just because El Niño is a familiar cycle doesn’t mean things will be the same when this one is over.

entries.title: How Did Trump’s Trade Fight With Canada Go So Sideways?
entries.summary: And why does the president loathe Canada but respect North Korea?
entries.content:
And why does the president loathe Canada but respect North Korea?

Check your local listings, watch full episodes

here, or listen to the weekly podcast

here.

In 1999, the creators of South Park were nominated for an Academy Award for their song “Blame Canada.” “South Park, of course, is caustic and anarchic satire. But today, somehow, it’s become real,” the editor in chief of The Atlantic, Jeffrey Goldberg, said last night on Washington Week With The Atlantic.

What started as a fight over trade has gone dangerously, ridiculously sideways. Why does President Trump loathe Canada but respect North Korea? What might NATO members be thinking about Trump’s treatment of his supposed allies?

Joining Goldberg to discuss these questions and more: Stephen Hayes of The Dispatch, Idrees Kahloon of The Atlantic, Ashley Parker of The Atlantic, and Josh Wingrove of Bloomberg News.

Watch the full episode here.
